title: How 9/11 Changed New York—And America
excerpt: Photographs by Sasha Arutyunova L ike most New Englanders of a certain generation, my parents viewed New York City with distrust
body: Photographs by Sasha Arutyunova L ike most New Englanders of a certain generation, my parents viewed New York City with distrust
They associated their neighbor to the south with “The Bronx Is Burning,” Bernhard Goetz, blackouts, bankruptcy, and the famous New York Daily News headline Ford to City: Drop Dead
The heart of Manhattan was a decadent playground for the wealthy, while outlying neighborhoods were plagued by desperate poverty and violence
I grew up only 200 miles away, and yet my parents never took me there as a kid
But if New York felt menacing and foreign to them, in reality, it is the most American of cities
New York is a symbol of the nation’s money and power, its diversity and freedom
It is our capital of culture, a proudly loud and bustling melting pot
And for those who wanted to humble the world’s sole superpower, New York was the perfect place to strike 25 years ago this week
Two of its signature skyscrapers were toppled, and nearly 3,000 lives were lost
The response underscored how much New York belongs to America
Rescue workers from red and blue states raced to help
Donations poured in from rich California cities and small Montana towns
For the first time in decades, and less than a year after a bitterly contested presidential election, the nation felt unified
We’ve been chasing that feeling ever since
New York City has bounced back—revitalized and thriving—with a new skyline emerging from the dust
But the nation is deeply divided, with angrier elections and escalating political violence
The pandemic could have brought the sort of unity we felt after the terror attacks, but it instead largely fostered division and rage
There is a new conflict in the Middle East, one whose dubious origins evoke the misguided war launched there after the World Trade Center fell
And now, a quarter century after the September 11 attacks, a New Yorker is president, one who was in Manhattan that crystal-clear, late-summer day
But Donald Trump won’t be there on Friday
M y first visit to New York City included the World Trade Center
I was in high school when, in 1995, my brother and I joined a church-group trip down from Massachusetts (my parents still wanted no part of it) to Liberty and Ellis Islands
I remember the ferry ride back to Lower Manhattan at the day’s end, staring at those impossibly tall towers
Later, I was lucky enough to go to college in New York, and immersed myself in its energy

The Twin Towers were not exactly beloved architecture, but they were a constant, comforting presence; when you got out of the subway downtown, below the city’s street grid, the easiest way to orient yourself was to locate the World Trade Center
Find those towers, and you could get yourself anywhere
Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic On September 11, 2001, I was a 21-year-old intern at the New York Daily News and, with no money to my name, was between apartments and sleeping on my friend’s couch
It was Primary Day, and I had the morning off ahead of covering some comptroller candidate’s Election Night party
My friend’s nanny had the television on, and I heard her shriek
Al-Qaeda got what it wanted: As the world watched the first tower burn, the second was hit
I grabbed my notebook and tried to get to work
But I was staying uptown, at West 120th Street, and the subways were already a mess and soon shut completely
I couldn’t reach the newspaper’s assignment desk; the phones were overloaded
So I started walking south, toward the World Trade Center, trying to listen to updates on my portable radio
Not long after the towers fell, I connected with an editor who diverted me to a major hospital with a trauma center, to witness the arrival of the injured
I was instead confronted by a jarring and heartbreaking image: rows of empty hospital beds
The scores of survivors never came; there simply weren’t many
When the wind turned, I could smell the smoke, an acrid blend of jet fuel and steel and other things too sad to consider
My next stop, after nightfall, was a bereavement center set up farther downtown
I fielded as many questions as I asked, and desperate pleas from frantic people—some covered in ash—looking for information about their missing loved ones

title: All the Places Trump Was on 9/11
excerpt: ET on September 9, 2026 W here were you on 9/11? Every American old enough to remember the day has an answer to that question
body: ET on September 9, 2026 W here were you on 9/11? Every American old enough to remember the day has an answer to that question

At a ceremony honoring first responders and victims’ families yesterday, Trump offered an elaborate account of where he was in the hours and days after nearly 3,000 Americans were killed. “I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened, and they had no hesitation; everybody went down with me
Wasn’t too much we could do, I’ll be honest
It was raw—nobody had seen anything like it, ever.” The story presents significant problems in terms of its relationship to reality

Listeners could be forgiven for interpreting Trump’s remarks as a reference to his whereabouts on the day of the attack itself. (The president clarified that timeline last night: “I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.) It is true that two days after the attack, on September 13, Trump was interviewed by reporters while walking in Lower Manhattan

The president has previously made variations of the same claim—that he and the employees he sent downtown helped clear rubble in the days following the attack. “Everyone who helped clear the rubble—and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit” was his version of it on the 2016 campaign trail
But supporting evidence is scant, and the whole account is likely an exaggeration

Richard Alles, a retired New York City Fire Department deputy chief who had a supervisory role in the efforts, said in 2019 not only that he never witnessed Trump at the site, but that the account doesn’t add up: “He was a private citizen at the time

I don’t know what kind of role he could have possibly played.” And, Alles added , if Trump had indeed sent workers, as he has claimed, there would be a record of it: “Is there a chance he was ever down there by himself and I didn’t know it? It’s possible, but I know of no one who ever witnessed him there.” Nevertheless, Trump pressed on, veering into territory even further detached from verifiable fact
Steel Building—a skyscraper in Lower Manhattan known today as One Liberty Plaza—was “really creaking,” Trump said at yesterday’s ceremony. “I’ll never forget: two firemen
We thought it was coming down on top of us and two firemen—big, strong guys
And I’m not the smallest guy in the world
They grabbed me under the arms, said, ‘Gotta get outta here.’ And they literally lifted me up—this is not easy to do; I’m big
They lifted me up, and they started running with me
I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself.’ But they were amazing, but they thought it was coming down
Steel.” There was, in fact, public concern in the days following the attack that the building at One Liberty Plaza could collapse
But the notion that Trump was inside the building and rushed out by firefighters has not been corroborated by any evidence
The president has offered versions of the same account before, though in less colorful form
In 2016, he told a story about being evacuated by firefighters—but in that rendition, it took place “a couple of days” after the collapse, and the U.S
Steel building was “not so far from us” when the two “massive guys” grabbed him. “I never knew I could run that fast,” he said then
In 2021, Trump likewise recalled two firemen grabbing him after hearing “creaks.” Trump’s whereabouts on September 11 are no mystery
They are fairly well documented by his own prior statements about watching the attacks unfold from his home in Trump Tower, about four miles north of the Twin Towers

For those who have reason to doubt Trump’s statements, his whereabouts are also documented on video. “I have a window that looks directly at the World Trade Center, and I saw this huge explosion,” he said in a phone interview with a New Jersey news channel on 9/11. “For years, I’ve looked right directly at the building—I’d see the Empire State Building in the foreground and the World Trade Center in the background—and now I’m looking at absolutely nothing
It’s just gone, and it’s just hard to believe.” Trump’s view may have been clear, but his recollection of September 11 has been murky, as reporters have tracked for more than a decade

Sometimes, in his accounts, he watched the second plane hit the World Trade Center from his apartment in Trump Tower; when he called into the live broadcast that day, he did not mention having witnessed the second jet

Sometimes, he claims to have personally seen people jumping from the Twin Towers. “I have a window in my apartment that specifically was aimed at the World Trade Center,” he said in 2015 on the campaign trail, “and I watched as people jumped.” In his TV interview the day of the attack, he didn’t see those scenes himself but talked to someone who had. “I have somebody that was down there who witnessed at least 10 people jumping out of the building from 70 and 80 stories up in the air,” Trump said

The president has also embellished what he saw in news coverage on that day, most notoriously claiming to have seen widespread celebrations by Muslim residents in New Jersey. “I watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down,” he said in a 2015 stump speech. “And I watched in Jersey City, New Jersey, where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down.” That claim has been thoroughly disproved

A professor who spent months combing through news reels and video archives from that day found one possible instance that could slightly resemble those events—a few Arab American teenagers who briefly gathered in front of a library in South Paterson in a way that could be seen as celebratory
Even the live phone interview Trump participated in on the day of the attack contains inaccuracies

On the call, Trump said that one of his buildings was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan: “Forty Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan,” he said when asked whether his property had been damaged. “When they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest
And now it’s the tallest.” But as The Washington Post documented , using data from the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat, neither claim was true
Forty Wall Street was the tallest building for only about two years and that was in the 1930s, before Trump was born
A t the center of yesterday’s ceremony was an important honor—one that Trump had promised to bestow months prior

Welles Crowther, who was first identified as “the man in the red bandana” in a 2002 New York Times story, rescued more than a dozen people from the South Tower before being killed when the building collapsed

His parents, who had given him a red bandana as a boy and knew that he always carried it with him, were able to recognize him by that detail and confirmed through the survivors that their son had helped them
Crowther was an equities trader and a volunteer firefighter, and he was 24 years old when he died

While awarding a posthumous Presidential Medal of Freedom to Crowther, Trump drew the focus to himself, comparing his own fame to that of the fallen hero: “The Man in the Red Bandana, he’s become more famous than me—I don’t like it

But he’s become much more famous than me.” [ Read: Trump is putting his face on everything ] When the president has brought up 9/11 lately, the remark has usually been severed from the attack, its victims, or its perpetrators
This year, Trump has tended to mention the day in the context of lambasting political opponents

He’s invoked it on several recent occasions—alongside World War I, World War II, and Pearl Harbor—when arguing that the attack and all three of those historical calamities are dwarfed by the danger communism poses to America today

title: Does Trump Want Republicans to Win the Midterms?
excerpt: Is Donald Trump trying to help Republicans win the midterm elections? The obvious answer to this question is yes, of course , simply because all political leade
body: Is Donald Trump trying to help Republicans win the midterm elections? The obvious answer to this question is yes, of course , simply because all political leaders benefit from their party winning elections
Yet several of Trump’s actions throw this normally perfunctory question into at least some doubt
Traditionally, candidates laboring under the burden of an unpopular president seek to detach themselves from the national brand
He has launched a national ad campaign focused on himself, and thrown a high-profile “midterm convention” designed to further reinforce the synonymity of the party and its leader

Trump has also made several remarks that convey an emotional detachment from the election’s outcome—comments such as “I’m not affected by the election” or “I don’t care about the midterms.” Perhaps he is merely feigning indifference
More likely, Trump cares about the outcome, but not enough to permit Republicans to acknowledge his lack of popularity
His approach, at any rate, nicely illustrates the drawbacks of handing total control of a political party to an egomaniac
Midterm elections have historically disfavored the president’s party

Candidates for office who are running in neutral or hostile territory accordingly tend to emphasize their differences with the president—think of Joe Manchin running an ad in West Virginia in 2010 showing him firing an actual bullet at Barack Obama’s cap-and-trade bill, or the Republican Will Hurd in 2018 criticizing Trump’s racism and affinity for Russia. [ Listen: Trump’s economy goes to the polls ] Trump’s public standing is unusually dire
He is currently polling far worse than either he did at this point in 2018 or Joe Biden did four years ago
In theory, this ought to give Republicans an especially strong incentive to edge away from Trump and emphasize local themes in their elections
Trump has decided to block this escape route
He is commandeering earned media with his “Trumpapalooza” show, drawing attention to the person endangered Republicans desperately need their constituents to forget
He has hoarded the party’s ad budget, warning Republicans, “This is my money that I control,” and that he would spend it on “Republicans that I think are good,” which is to say, slavishly loyal
He has promised to barnstorm the country, telling reporters, “I’ll be making a lot of stops,” including in Alaska, where the Republican Dan Sullivan is trailing
There is an old Simpsons episode in which the elderly oligarch Montgomery Burns informs the obsequious Smithers that, upon his own death, his loyal aide will be buried alive at his boss’s feet
Trump appears to be thinking along similar lines
This self-defeating behavior makes a degree of sense if you accept that Trump’s interest in politics is purely egocentric
He has difficulty caring about anything that does not directly involve himself, and the prospect of Republicans holding seats by repudiating his record is likely unpalatable
The benefits of same-party control of Congress are also smaller for Trump than other presidents, because he governs mainly through executive action
To the extent that a Democratic majority in either chamber might threaten him with oversight, he will surely disregard it, as he did during his first term
Although he finds Republican majorities preferable, the size of those majorities matters to him far less than their composition—a fully loyal minority may seem preferable to a fractious majority
What makes less sense is the willingness of many Republicans to cooperate with a strategy that consigns many of them to defeat
Consider, for instance, Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan
Rogers came up through politics long before Trump entered it, and is trying to win office in a state where the president’s approval rating is 25 points underwater
A recent poll of the state found Trump’s endorsement made voters less likely, by a 55 percent to 27 percent margin, to support a candidate
Yet Rogers has opened no daylight whatsoever with the unpopular president, even echoing his false claims of having the 2020 election stolen from him
When Trump launched a trade war with Canada, a move that poses an especially dire threat to Rogers’s own state, he declined to take the opportunity to display independence

Instead, he issued a statement mumbling his approval. (“President Trump is right to put America First—and tariffs are necessary, but are not a one-size-fits-all solution . ”) The same dynamic is occurring in other races, where Trump is throwing himself behind incumbents who are in danger mainly because voters don’t like him. [ Read: Trump plans to buy midterm ads about his own record ] To be sure, some Republicans subscribe to the theory that the Trump era has suspended normal midterm election dynamics
According to this account, a decisive sliver of voters are loyal to Trump, and not his party

Republicans can win only by enticing them to vote, which means making the election about their hero. “We’ve seen that a lot of Trump voters—they will crawl over glass to vote for the president,” one Republican strategist explained to Politico
Yet Trump has tried before to insert himself into non-presidential elections

And his efforts have mostly failed—not only in the 2018 midterms, when he refused to lie low, but also in multiple off-schedule elections (the most famous case being Georgia’s 2021 Senate runoff, which he made into a referendum on his effort to overturn the 2020 election)

In the Trump era, his party has fared well only when it has been able to focus on the shortcomings of unpopular Democratic opponents, such as Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Biden and Kamala Harris in 2024
Making elections about Trump—which also occurred when he ran for reelection in 2020—has been a losing gambit
The political tip sheets in recent days have been filled with the lamentations of fatalistic Republican operatives. “We have no choice
We’re stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not,” a top Republican campaign official confessed to Axios

They cannot stop Trump from staging Trumpapalooza, so they are reduced to praying for low ratings. “My only hope is that no one watches it since it’s competing versus NFL opening games,” a person close to the White House told Politico . “Hopefully nobody notices the embarrassing show.” Republicans are cooperating in a strategy that sacrifices their best chance of political survival, because the past decade has trained them to believe that resistance to Trump is futile

Trump did far less damage to the country during his first term, both because institutions and norm-following officials restrained him, and because his pathological instincts frequently undermined his support
The former limitation has broken down in the second term, but the latter one remains

title: Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
excerpt: © Jenny Stock / Ocean Photographer of the Year Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award
body: © Jenny Stock / Ocean Photographer of the Year Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award

An American crocodile moves through the mangroves of Cuba, a habitat that provides shelter for crocodiles feeding, breeding, nesting, and raising their young. © Marc Lenfant / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Adventure
Three surfers converge on the same wave at Teahupoʻo, French Polynesia, after a paddler is thrown from his board
The tow-in surfer immediately changes course, grabbing the cameraman to avoid a collision. © Julien Anton / Ocean Photographer of the Year Overall Winner, Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
An adult seahorse pictured with newly born juveniles in the shallow seaweed-filled waters of Moorea, French Polynesia

While it is not known whether these seahorses are related, their arrangement creates the impression of a farewell, as if the tiny seahorses have gathered around their father after he has released them into the world. © Ajiex Dharma / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Fine Art

A hinge-back cleaning shrimp rests against a pink barrel sponge in Bali, Indonesia; its eyes are sharply focused while the surrounding colors dissolve into a soft blur. © Jenny Stock / Ocean Photographer of the Year Winner, Female Fifty Fathoms Award
A mother humpback whale and her calf glide through Tonga’s warm, sheltered waters
The calf stays close to its mother at first, then becomes curious, swimming in playful circles and approaching the camera
The mother remains calm and watchful, guiding her young when it comes too close. © Romain Barats / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Impact
Three gentoo penguins stand beside the rusting remains of the former Hektor whaling station at Whalers Bay, Deception Island, Antarctica
Once a center for Antarctic whaling, the site is now being reclaimed by wildlife and the harsh polar environment. © Lars von Ritter Zahony / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Adventure
Sunlight pours through cracks in an iceberg in East Greenland, illuminating the seabed like a natural theater
Created by a storm just days earlier, these openings allow light to reach an underwater world usually hidden in darkness. © Allan Cronin / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Wildlife
A New Zealand fur seal tears apart a rough skate in the waters of New Zealand, while seabirds gather for the scraps
Unable to swallow such large prey whole, the seal throws the skate repeatedly to break it into smaller pieces. © James Ferrara / Ocean Photographer of the Year Second Place, Fine Art
A common octopus reveals its intricate suckers, textured skin, and watchful eye in the waters of Blue Heron Bridge, Florida

Known for its rich marine life, this shallow dive site provided the setting for a close encounter with one of the ocean’s most intelligent animals. © Richard Condlyffe / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Fine Art
A ladybug amphipod, only 3 millimeters long, rests on a blue sea squirt in the coral reefs of Komodo, Indonesia. © Gergo Rugli / Ocean Photographer of the Year Third Place, Human Connection
A teenager stands at Bronte Ocean Pool, Sydney, as a powerful swell sends waves crashing over the closed bathing site
While the conditions forced beaches to shut, people watched the waves from behind the fence

A group of locals climbed into the closed area and stood on the edge, waiting for the waves to crash over them and sweep them across the pool. c© Thomas Pavy / Ocean Photographer of the Year First Place, Conservation Hope
A great hammerhead shark, known as Tamataroa in French Polynesia, is photographed at 55 meters depth in Tiputa Pass, Rangiroa Atoll, during a population survey
This image represents the moment an anonymous shark becomes a known individual

Through photo identification and laser-calibrated video photogrammetry, scientists can track sharks over time to measure their size, sex, and population trends. © Leighton Lum / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Hope
A Hawaiian monk seal rests with her week-old pup on Kaimana Beach in Waikīkī

Mothers nurse their pups for around six weeks without feeding, losing up to a third of their body weight while the pup grows before becoming independent. © Lin Yongxuan / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Hope

At sunrise, a traditional fishing village shares the coastline with rows of oﬀshore wind turbines stretching across the sea, on Nanri Island, Fujian, China. © James Ferrara / Ocean Photographer of the Year First Place, Conservation Impact
A whale shark is surrounded by divers and snorkelers in the Maldives, revealing the overwhelming pressure that crowded wildlife tourism can place on marine animals
With almost 50 people visible in the frame, this image captures the reality behind some popular wildlife encounters: an animal seeking space while people compete for a closer view
It challenges us to rethink how we experience and protect the species we admire. © Yuta Shigeno / Ocean Photographer of the Year Third Place, Conservation Hope
A male white-spotted puﬀerfish creates an intricate spawning nest in the sand
The fish carefully shapes a two-meter-wide radial pattern using only his fins

Built over several days, this structure and its subtle details reveal the extraordinary eﬀort this small fish invests in reproduction. © Iris Uijttewaal / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Ocean Unseen
A pygmy seahorse, no larger than a grain of rice, clings to a delicate hydroid in the reefs of Raja Ampat, Indonesia
Perfectly camouflaged, these tiny animals are rarely seen, even by experienced divers. © Daniel Taylor / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Conservation Impact
A silky shark circles helplessly after taking bait from an illegal longline, its fate sealed by a steel hook and heavy line designed to prevent escape
Photographed less than 48 hours after Baja California’s seasonal shark-fishing ban ended, the image reveals a hidden reality unfolding far from shore

A small group of pilot fish remains beside the shark, highlighting how the loss of one animal can ripple throughout an entire ecosystem. © Chen Lin / Ocean Photographer of the Year Finalist, Human Connection
From above, moored fishing and tourist boats bloom across the sapphire-blue sea, like the petals of a flower

title: Inside the White House on 9/11
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by John McConnell, the longtime
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by John McConnell, the longtime senior speechwriter for President George W
Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney, to discuss their memories of September 11, 2001—25 years later
Then, David ends with a discussion of American Pastoral, a novel by Philip Roth, and what we can learn about domestic terrorism from the book

The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Well, what I remember, that’s actually maybe one of my most vivid memories of the day, is stepping out of that building and Washington is deserted, and there’s yellow tape everywhere marking off the streets, and there’s the National Guard and armored personnel carriers everywhere
They’ll be lowered the next—I remember thinking, They will be lowered tomorrow
But tonight they’re high. [ Music ] Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be John McConnell, a colleague of mine in the George W
Bush speechwriting department, and himself chief speechwriter to former Vice President Dick Cheney
We’ll be talking about 9/11 at the quarter-century anniversary
John and I spent much of the day together on 9/11, 2001—and we’ll be discussing what we saw, what we thought, what we felt, and what we did
The book discussion this week will also be terrorism-related: the novel American Pastoral by Philip Roth, his discussion of a homegrown terrorist in Roth’s own native state of New Jersey
Before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some home news
We’re going to be conducting an experiment here in The David Frum Show with a new tempo

Twice a week: releasing one show on Wednesday, the show you see, which will contain an interview and a book discussion, and a shorter show, which we’ll be releasing each Saturday on both YouTube and on whatever audio platform you use: Spotify, Apple, whatever it is
The second show, the Saturday show, will be much shorter—no interview, just some thoughts from me on the events of the week just passed
And the first of the shows, which we’ll release this coming Saturday, I will offer my own reflections on the 25th anniversary of 9/11
The United States has been almost unceasingly at war in the Middle East since 9/11, 2001
And I’ll be offering some of my thoughts about how I think about that experience, how others might want to think about it, whatever information I can offer
I played a small part in that history, and I think about it almost all the time, and I’ll be sharing those thoughts with you
And we’ll be continuing each Saturday after that
I do hope you’ll join and will bookmark us or subscribe to The Atlantic YouTube channel, or whatever audio channel you use, so you will not miss any of our Saturday shows
I hope you will join me this coming Saturday and each successive Saturday for the second, shorter David Frum Show weekend episode
And now my dialogue with John McConnell. [ Music ] Frum: My guest today is John McConnell
John is one of the greatest speechwriters in American history, but that’s only incidentally why I’ve invited him today
Bush administration, and I spent much of September 11th, 2001, in his company, sharing emotions of shock, dismay, and grief
As we mark the 25th anniversary of a tragic day, I wanted to be with him again
John wrote for Vice President Dan Quayle, then for the Bob Dole for President campaign in 1996
Bush campaign in 2000 and then did remarkable service in the Bush White House, where he doubled as both a writer for the president and the sole speechwriter for Vice President Richard Cheney
John was a pallbearer at Vice President Cheney’s funeral

It was his frequent writing partner, Matt Scully, who delivered the finest verdict on John’s work: “As a general rule in Bush speeches, if the writing is graceful, judicious, and understated and makes you think about the subject at hand instead of anyone’s particular craftsmanship or religiosity, there’s a better-than-even chance it is by John McConnell.” It’s John’s lifelong reflex to deflect attention from himself, but today he must overcome that reflex and accept his place in American history
Frum: So we spent the day together on 9/11
Let me start by asking you to summon your memories of what happened that day, where you were at, from the beginning to the end
McConnell: I was sitting outside Vice President Cheney’s inner office door in the West Wing
The night before, Matthew Scully and I had been working on a speech for the president for the end of that week
And at the end of Monday, I looked at my list of things to do, and I realized that Cheney had a speech on Friday too, and I thought, Well, I haven’t given this much thought
I said, Can I pop in on him tomorrow morning? And she said, How much time do you need? I said, Ten minutes, maybe five
I just wanted to ask him about his speech
And so the next morning—you remember how we’d get to the office, and the president’s and vice president’s schedules would be under our doors
And I looked at it; it said, “Meeting with John McConnell, 8:30,” and I thought, Oh, well, it’s an official meeting, so I really better be there at 8:30 sharp

title: The Inside Story of What Happened at Stars and Stripes
excerpt: A “chicken plate,” in military parlance, is a protective shield used in a variety of combat situations
body: A “chicken plate,” in military parlance, is a protective shield used in a variety of combat situations
During the Vietnam War, chicken plates were inserted into vests—they are resistant against small-arms fire, but they’re also bulky and hot
So some pilots sat on them instead, which had the added benefit of providing protection against bullets that came from below
I first encountered another type of chicken plate in Iraq, where I was embedded with a convoy of American service members patrolling outside of Tikrit
On this particular morning, I sat alongside three soldiers inside an up-armored Humvee while a gunner manned the turret
But that gunner—James Murphy, a sergeant from New Jersey—wasn’t sitting in his sling, which was little more than a seat-belt strap hooked between two sides of the turret
If he sat down, the chicken plate would block his view
This left Murphy with a choice: stand up for hours and expose his head and chest, or remain behind the plate’s limited protection and endanger the convoy by missing a threat
For the dozen or so gunners I spoke with, the choice was clear
Two of them removed the chicken plate entirely for a better view
The military had no specific data on gunner casualties or whether the chicken plates were preventing them
Yet an Army general in Iraq was asking his staff why they were losing so many gunners

One officer I spoke with at the time told me that the answer was obvious the moment someone stood in the turret. [ Tom Nichols: Hegseth’s Pentagon lurches off the rails ] I reported a series of stories on gunners for Stars and Stripes , a newspaper with a long history of editorial independence despite being housed within the Department of Defense

A few weeks later, after returning to my home at the time—a room at the bachelor officers’ quarters on a Marine Corps base in Okinawa—I received a message from our Pentagon beat reporter, who told me that military officials had read the series and were fast-tracking improved equipment for deployment
They’d found a way to help protect the gunners without blocking their view from the turret
At least some military officials were aware of the issue and had been testing prototypes for better shields
But many of the soldiers weren’t willing to discuss with senior leaders the specifics of what they needed, out of concern that they’d be viewed as complaining
I’m grateful that they trusted me enough to tell their stories
Looking back now, what feels remarkable isn’t the lack of proper equipment
It’s the way the Pentagon was willing to take independent journalism that spotlighted deficiencies and use it to improve conditions for service members
Uniformed military leaders have not lost the means to analyze and act on useful journalism
But publicly denouncing the reporting or the news outlet makes it far less likely that they will
Attacking people for telling the truth creates a chilling effect for truth tellers—including those who are themselves in the military
The best journalism unearths information that complex bureaucracies overlook or suppress, intentionally or not
When leaders treat asking tough questions and reporting uncomfortable facts as disloyalty, they devalue a tool that can help them fix crucial problems
The danger in this devaluation is immense, especially now; it comes as U.S. service members are once again fighting in the Middle East
The Pentagon hasn’t held a press briefing on combat operations in Iran since May 5
The Correspondents’ Corridor, where reporters worked inside the Pentagon for decades, is closed while court appeals continue on press-access restrictions

The New York Times is suing the Pentagon on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the Pentagon’s attempts to prevent independent reporting are clearly unconstitutional. (I should disclose that I, too, am suing the Pentagon
I was fired after I said in an appearance on CBS News that my personal red line would be if the Pentagon ever instructed me not to publish a perfectly accurate story

It is telling that I am being fired for describing the most anodyne of journalistic ethics, a position that any self-respecting reporter in any free society would hold, and that the Pentagon interpreted as insubordination.) Stars and Stripes has its roots in the Civil War, when Union soldiers took over a printing press in Bloomfield, Missouri
The paper was revived during World War I under General John “Black Jack” Pershing and has published continuously since 1942, when General George C

Marshall recognized the value it provided troops and aimed to follow Pershing’s example. “No official control was ever exercised over the matter which went into” Stars and Stripes , Marshall said of the WWI edition
It didn’t take long for that editorial freedom to be challenged

General George Patton complained about the “Willie and Joe” cartoonist Bill Mauldin’s depictions of soldiers as they often appeared—tired and dirty. (Mauldin would have known; he was himself a soldier.) But General Dwight Eisenhower rejected Patton’s drive to control the reporting itself. “It is the soldier’s paper,” he said, “and we won’t interfere,” according to the historian Stephen Ambrose’s foreword in a book by Mauldin, whose wartime cartoons earned him the 1945 Pulitzer Prize
The newspaper continued to operate overseas after World War II, hiring civilian journalists to work alongside service members
But attempts at curtailing Stripes ’ independence periodically arose
Congress documented occasional pressures in the 1960s

In the ’80s, a General Accounting Office report to Congress found conclusive evidence of censorship, and pointed out the “inherent cultural conflict” between the First Amendment mission and the military’s own

Those findings led the House Armed Services Committee to direct the Pentagon to establish an ombudsman, responsible to Congress, who would monitor the free flow of information to service members through Stars and Stripes

title: Batteries just broke another record in the US
excerpt: Record-breaking quarter: US battery installations hit 20.2 gigawatt-hours in the second quarter of 2026, putting the country on track for a 20% year-over-year i
body: Record-breaking quarter: US battery installations hit 20.2 gigawatt-hours in the second quarter of 2026, putting the country on track for a 20% year-over-year increase in total capacity

Big projects are doing the heavy lifting: Seven gigascale battery installations (those with a capacity over one gigawatt-hour) came online in just three months, with utility-scale systems driving most of the growth

Home batteries are stumbling: Commercial installations are growing because of data centers, but residential installations are projected to fall 16% in 2026. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143680" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Battery installations hit a new record in the US in the second quarter of 2026
In total, 20.2 gigawatt-hours of new capacity came online, according to a new report
That’s enough to supply the daily electricity needs of about 700,000 homes
The surge is putting the country on a trajectory to see 71 gigawatt-hours of batteries installed in 2026, a 20% increase over last year

This growth is being driven by a combination of cheaper batteries and an urgent need for more energy storage capacity as renewables such as solar and onshore wind power are added to the grid.  Massive, utility-scale systems are leading the way; they’re responsible for most of the record-setting quarter

Seven new gigascale battery installations (those with a capacity of over one gigawatt-hour) came online during the three-month stretch, according to the report , published by Benchmark Mineral Intelligence and the Solar Energy Industries Association. “It really came down to a handful of big projects,” says Shan Tomouk, energy storage and energy lead for Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
But there was also growth in the category of so-called behind-the-meter batteries, which include both residential and industrial battery storage systems

These projects, generally smaller than utility-scale installations, are typically owned and operated by homeowners or businesses rather than utilities or power providers.  In the behind-the-meter category, data centers led the way, making up about three-quarters of new batteries in the commercial sector
But residential batteries saw a sharp slowdown
These systems are often installed in homes to store power from solar panels or serve as a backup source in case of a blackout
Home installations are projected to drop by 16% in 2026 compared with last year, according to the report
That drop happened largely because a tax credit that helped subsidize home battery systems ended in 2025, Tomouk says
Home installations should recover by the end of the decade, he adds
And tax credits for nonresidential batteries have largely survived
Overall, batteries are a bright spot in energy right now. “This is one of the strong sectors in the US,” says Isshu Kikuma, an energy storage analyst at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy
As the battery market continues to grow, one major trend to keep an eye on is a move toward US-made technology
Today, nearly all the systems coming online use cells made in China, though some are put together into complete energy storage systems in the US
Tariffs were already pushing the US energy storage industry toward domestic production
And beginning this year, energy storage tax credits required projects to limit their reliance on batteries imported from China
There’s a lot of manufacturing capacity set to come online in the US, though these factories probably won’t be able to meet demand until at least 2030 or so, Tomouk says, so prices could tick up.

title: Understanding the thermal ceiling in portable power
excerpt: Plug a phone into a modern charger and the first 10 minutes are impressive
body: Plug a phone into a modern charger and the first 10 minutes are impressive
It’s the connected device protecting itself

As temperature rises during charging, a smartphone’s battery management system reduces the current it will accept, because heat accelerates the chemical degradation that permanently reduces battery capacity
The charger may be capable of delivering more, but the device simply stops taking it
For anyone building products in the portable power category, this creates an uncomfortable gap between specification and experience
A device rated at 25 watts is accurate in the sense that it can deliver 25 watts
Whether it delivers 25 watts for the duration of a charge is a different question, and one the specification does not answer
The specification gap The gap matters commercially because it is invisible at the point of purchase and obvious in use
Consumers compare wattage figures on packaging
They don’t compare thermal curves, because thermal curves are not published publicly

The result is a category where products differentiate on a number that describes peak output rather than sustained output, and where the actual user experience of two products with identical specifications can diverge substantially
This is particularly acute in magnetic wireless charging

Inductive power transfer generates heat at both the transmitting and receiving coils, and the magnetic attachment that makes these products convenient also places the heat source in direct contact with the device it is charging
Convenience and thermal performance are working against each other by design
The industry’s response for the past several years has been materials science
Graphite sheets, thermal interface materials, conductive housings, and heat-spreading layers have all improved how efficiently accumulated heat moves away from the source
Each generation has been incrementally better than the last
But passive dissipation has a structural limitation: it can only move heat that has already been generated, and only as fast as the surrounding air will accept it
In a sealed, pocket-sized enclosure, that ceiling arrives quickly
Improving the materials slows the rate of temperature rise

Moving from dissipation to removal The alternative is active thermal management, which is standard in stationary electronics and largely absent from portable ones for reasons that are easy to understand
Fans add volume, weight, moving parts, and noise
In a product category defined by portability, each of those is a meaningful cost
At Anker, which manufactures charging and power products, engineering teams spent the past several development cycles working on whether that tradeoff could be made acceptable rather than eliminated

The approach involves several interacting systems: a micro centrifugal fan, dual airflow channels routed to avoid interference with the magnetic array, a three-layer graphene heat-spreading layer, and a control algorithm that modulates fan speed based on real-time temperature and battery state rather than running at a fixed rate
The result is that the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro has become the world’s fastest and coolest wireless power bank

In internal testing, at 77 °F (25 °C) ambient, the back of the power bank stays below 96.8 °F (36 °C) throughout wireless charging, 21.6 °F (12 °C) below the international standard limit of 118.4 °F (48 °C), for a comfortable grip
Comparable magnetic power banks in the same testing typically reached 113 °F (45 °C) or higher within 20 minutes

The functional consequence is that the connected device does not reach the threshold at which it begins reducing charge acceptance, so 25 watts of Qi2.2 magnetic wireless charging is delivered as a working rate rather than an opening rate
In practice, an iPhone 17 Pro reaches 50% charge in 25 minutes
The Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro’s premium performance in both charging speed and thermal management is certified by SGS, an independent testing and certification company
Recharging a power bank generates heat too, which is why devices in this category are often slow to recharge, leaving users with an empty accessory at the moment they need it
Active cooling during input allows the unit to accept 45 watts and reach 80% in 52 minutes
What this suggests about the category There is a broader pattern here worth naming, because it is not unique to charging
When a category improves along a single axis for long enough, the constraint usually migrates somewhere else
Charging spent a decade optimizing power delivery
Power delivery is now, for most practical purposes, solved: the electronics can supply more energy than the receiving device is willing to accept
The binding constraint moved to thermal management, and the industry continued optimizing the axis it had always optimized, because that is the axis the specifications describe
Recognizing when a constraint has moved is difficult precisely because the old metric keeps improving
Products have continued to get faster on paper

title: What OpenAI’s latest controversy tells us about the future of math
excerpt: A milestone wrapped in controversy: OpenAI claims to have solved one of mathematics' most prestigious unsolved problems, the Navier–Stokes existence and sm
body: A milestone wrapped in controversy: OpenAI claims to have solved one of mathematics' most prestigious unsolved problems, the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, but the announcement has been overshadowed by accusations that the company built on two researchers' work without crediting them

Math's uncomfortable new reality: OpenAI solved in days what two humans spent nearly a year on, deploying 10,000 simultaneous AI agents at a cost of millions—resources no academic mathematician could ever access, raising hard questions about who math's future actually belongs to

Something is lost when AI wins: As Terence Tao has warned, the messy, public process of human mathematicians failing and iterating is itself valuable—and when private companies solve problems in secret, that generative chaos disappears along with the answer. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143747" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> OpenAI’s latest mathematical milestone has quickly become mired in controversy
Today, the company announced that its agents have solved one of the Millennium Prize Problems, some of the most important open problems in mathematics
Under normal circumstances, that solution would be a huge feather in OpenAI’s cap

But the announcement has been overshadowed by accusations that OpenAI used NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster’s and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge’s AI-assisted work on the problem as a jumping-off point and failed to credit them

It remains uncertain if OpenAI’s models made use of the work completed by Buckmaster and Alpöge, though Sébastien Bubeck, a member of the technical staff at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the team was inspired to pursue the problem after hearing a rumor about Buckmaster and Alpöge’s efforts
But whether or not OpenAI’s models took advantage of Buckmaster and Alpöge’s research, this episode may mark a turning point in the history of mathematics

AI models now seem essential for making progress on the most important mathematical problems of our time, and solving them may demand resources only available at a couple of frontier AI companies, which often defy the norms of academic collaboration that undergird most mathematical progress

If that’s the future we are headed for, it is unclear how human mathematicians will fit into it.  The problem that OpenAI claims to have solved is known as the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem
It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000

Solutions come with a one million dollar prize; before today, only one other Millennium Prize Problem had been solved.  The Navier–Stokes problem concerns a set of equations that describes how fluids, such as water and air, flow over time
The equations are widely used in the field of fluid dynamics, and they have proven powerful, but physicists and mathematicians didn’t understand them completely
In particular, it was unknown until today whether the equations might, under some conditions, break down and predict an impossible state of affairs—such as a fluid having infinite velocity

On Monday, NYU’s Buckmaster posted a proof on the social media site Mastodon showing that a simplified version of the Navier–Stokes equations can indeed break down—a major step forward on the Millennium Problem
He and Alpöge had worked on the problem for almost a year, using publicly available models from both OpenAI and Anthropic
Then today, OpenAI presented a proof showing that the full Navier–Stokes equations can break down as well
The proof was obtained using an internal model that dramatically outperforms the already-impressive Astra model, which was only released last week
The company says it does not plan to claim the million-dollar prize for solving the problem
These mathematical achievements are indisputably impressive, but they have attracted far less attention than the controversy about their origins
Along with the proof, Buckmaster posted a document detailing his interactions with OpenAI employees after he heard rumors about their work and reached out to one of them

According to him, OpenAI employees presented two possibilities to him: Either he and Alpöge could post their work and OpenAI would post their Navier-Stokes solution the following day, or he could work with OpenAI on a Navier-Stokes paper that excluded Alpöge from authorship, due to his affiliation with Anthropic, OpenAI’s biggest rival

Buckmaster also wrote that he asked the employees whether the agents had obtained access to transcripts of the work that he and Alpöge had done with OpenAI models, which they denied; and whether OpenAI models had been trained on those transcripts, to which they offered no response
MIT Technology Review reached out to Buckmaster for comment, but didn’t hear back before publication
The clear implication of the document is that OpenAI’s models somehow made use of Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work
The Buckmaster/Alpöge and OpenAI proofs both make use of an approach to the Navier-Stokes problem pioneered by the mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa
According to Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematics professor at Brown University, this approach was one of several that was thought to hold promise for solving the Navier-Stokes problem
So, while it’s by no means impossible that both teams could have arrived at this approach independently, it’s also conceivable that Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work could have influenced OpenAI’s

In the press briefing, Mark Chen, OpenAI’s chief research officer, again denied that any agents or OpenAI employees accessed Buckmaster and Alpöge’s transcripts—but given what has been revealed about the Hugging Face hack , it’s clear that OpenAI is not always entirely aware of what its agents are doing.  If OpenAI’s models did train on Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work, or if its agents somehow gained access to it, then the company’s failure to track down the truth and assign those researchers appropriate credit reflects poorly on it

But there might be a thin silver lining to that version of the story for mathematicians, because it would suggest that the hard work of two humans, one of whom is a prominent expert on Navier-Stokes, was essential to the agents’ ability to solve the Millennium Problem
Experts have long identified “research taste,” or the ability to choose promising research questions and directions, as a major obstacle for AI in science and mathematics

If the OpenAI agents did indeed choose to follow the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa approach because Buckmaster and Alpöge had done the same, then human research taste played an essential role in OpenAI’s success
Even so, the bigger picture here is sobering
The progress that Buckmaster and Alpöge made over almost a year of collaboration with publicly available models speaks to the promise of human–AI collaboration
But they were not able to achieve a full solution

Meanwhile, OpenAI brute-forced a solution in a few days using an internal model, and their successful solution came at an astronomical cost: In the press briefing, Bubeck and Chen said the team was only able to solve the problem by running about 10,000 agents concurrently, at a cost of millions of dollars
Over the past few months, I’ve heard from several researchers that mathematicians are becoming depressed, and it’s not difficult to see why

Mathematics is quickly becoming the province of frontier AI companies with impressive internal-only models, money to burn, and a lack of collaborative spirit. “Whether AI companies will decide to spend their money on doing one thing or another, I truly don’t know,” says Gómez-Serrano. “What is clear is that very few mathematicians will have resources of that scale.” If OpenAI and Anthropic keep striving for more and more impressive mathematical accolades, there might not be any open problems left for human mathematicians outside of those companies to wrestle with
That would dramatically change the field of mathematics

Last week, UCLA mathematician Terence Tao wrote a Mastodon thread describing how important mistakes, wrong directions, and incomplete solutions are for the field. “In most cases in pure mathematics, the problems are posed not because we desperately want the solution to these problems in and of themselves, but because we have seen from past experience that human-directed efforts to solve these problems tend to spur further development of the field,” Tao wrote. “Prematurely solving the problem by purely AI-powered methods—particularly without full transparency into the solution process—can contaminate this process to the point where it actually becomes a net negative for the progress of mathematics as a whole.” Humans might take longer than agents to solve mathematical problems, but in the process, they uncover new mathematical approaches and ideas that might inspire their peers and even birth their own subfields

title: A journalist coined ‘the Bible Belt’ 100 years ago – it’s been oversimplifying the South ever since
url:
<title>A journalist coined ‘the Bible Belt’ 100 years ago – it’s been oversimplifying the South ever since</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758025/original/file-20260904-50-eaacuv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=18%2C0%2C6737%2C4491&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Even when the phrase was coined, the &#39;Bible Belt&#39; image depicted just a portion of the region&#39;s culture.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">John Hayes</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Look No Further!” a billboard on the side of the highway beckons, drawing my gaze toward the red cover of a Bible. “You Are Worthy of Redemption!”</p>

<p>Not far away, another sign urges me to “Keep Christ in Christmas.” Then farther down the road a third appears: “Jesus: COMING SOON” its bright colors announce.</p>

<p>Signs like these are familiar to me: I’m <a href="https://www.augusta.edu/faculty/directory/view.php?id=JHAYES22">a historian who studies the U.S. South</a> and lives in it. I know how easily they can evoke the South – or, I should say, a certain image of it. As that image pictures it, the South is “the Bible Belt”: a place where people are really religious, and, as a result, socially and politically conservative. Indeed, in this year of midterm elections, you’re almost certain to hear pundits invoke “the Bible Belt” as shorthand explanation for Southern political behavior.</p>

<p><a href="https://religionnews.com/2015/07/21/how-the-scopes-trial-created-the-bible-belt/">The phrase has been around for a century</a>. Its endurance, however – and the “evidence” behind it today – could use some serious scrutiny. I spotted those roadside signs, for example, in Ontario, Canada, a thousand miles from what anybody would think of as the South.</p>

<p>Of the many things said about the South over the years, “Bible Belt” is the cliché that just won’t die.</p>

<h2>Skewering the South</h2>

<p>“Bible Belt” entered the lexicon in 1924, <a href="https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015030748548&amp;seq=306&amp;q1=belt">in the pages of The American Mercury</a>, a magazine co-founded by H.L. Mencken. Based in Baltimore, at the upper edge of the South, Mencken was <a href="https://www.neh.gov/humanities/2014/novemberdecember/feature/h-l-mencken-boy-oh-boy">one of the nation’s most prominent journalists</a> in the decades between the world wars.</p>

<p>The acerbic satirist had skewered the South in his much-discussed 1919 essay “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/53467/pg53467-images.html#Page_136">The Sahara of the Bozart</a>,” depicting it as a vast cultural wasteland. In 1925, he closely covered the Dayton, Tennessee, trial of biology teacher John T. Scopes, who had been charged with violating the state’s law against <a href="https://theconversation.com/1-in-4-americans-reject-evolution-a-century-after-the-scopes-monkey-trial-spotlighted-the-clash-between-science-and-religion-258163">teaching Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution</a>. Mencken famously lampooned it as <a href="https://famous-trials.com/scopesmonkey/2132-menckenaccount">the Scopes “monkey trial</a>.”</p>

<p>He coined “Bible Belt” in his regular column of short news items, then employed the phrase routinely. By it he meant a place where two Protestant groups, the Baptists and the Methodists, dominated <a href="https://southernspaces.org/2004/religion-and-us-south/">not just religious life</a>, but also the mores of the whole society. The whole region, Mencken argued, was a Baptist-Methodist stranglehold where fun and free thought were banished.</p>

<h2>Whose Christianity?</h2>

<p>It’s true that in the early 20th century, Baptists and Methodists <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/515814">dominated the South in a way that they didn’t anywhere else</a>. To trace the bloc of states where over 50% of religious congregation members were Baptist or Methodist was to trace the region’s boundaries with uncanny precision.</p>

<p>But beneath commonalities, religious life was divided by both race and class. Black Baptists and Methodists met in their own churches: autonomous institutions that came to be known, collectively, as “<a href="https://theconversation.com/a-brief-history-of-the-black-churchs-diversity-and-its-vital-role-in-american-political-history-197511">the Black church</a>.” The region’s poor Christians drew on inherited traditions and their own hardships to <a href="https://uncpress.org/9781469635323/hard-hard-religion/">craft a folk version of Baptist-Methodist faith</a> – what I’ve written about as “hard, hard religion.” </p>

              <span class="caption">Members of the Primitive Baptist Church in Morehead, Ky., attend a creek baptism in 1940.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These religious divisions paralleled political ones. Through techniques like poll taxes and literacy tests, Southern states severely restricted the franchise, <a href="https://www.loc.gov/collections/civil-rights-history-project/articles-and-essays/voting-rights/">effectively stripping Black</a> and <a href="https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/amendments/amendment-xxiv/interpretations/157#the-twenty-fourth-amendment-by-deborah-archer-and-derek-muller">poor white</a> Southerners of their voting rights. </p>

<p>The social order that Mencken described as the Bible Belt, then, expressed the culture of elite and middle-class white people, the ones with the political power to enforce it. </p>

<p>“Bible Belt” joined other phrases that expressed how the early 20th-century South differed from national patterns. Amid industrializing, urbanizing America, <a href="https://reader.library.cornell.edu/docviewer/digital?id=chla2829610#page/153/mode/1up/search/odum">the South was “the Cotton Belt,”</a> the world’s leading cotton producer, with a predominantly rural, agricultural population. Political contests marked the nation, but in the “Solid South,” <a href="https://websites.umich.edu/%7Elawrace/votetour8.htm">the Democratic Party monopolized politics</a>. With high poverty, low wages and limited capital, the South was the prosperous nation’s “<a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/message-the-conference-economic-conditions-the-south">No. 1 economic problem</a>,” as President Franklin Roosevelt put it in 1938. And the violent racial oppression <a href="https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/origins.htm">of the “Jim Crow South”</a> was what many Black Southerners eagerly fled when doors of opportunity opened in other regions.</p>

<h2>A new South</h2>

<p>A century later, so much has changed.</p>

<p>Most Southerners, like most Americans, live in suburbs and <a href="https://statisticalatlas.com/region/South/Industries">work in a service economy</a>. Republicans <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/02/11/u-s-senate-has-fewest-split-delegations-since-direct-elections-began/">hold a political majority in the region</a>, but they have to compete for it. Southern-based corporations like Walmart, McKesson and Exxon Mobil are <a href="https://fortune.com/ranking/fortune500/">in the top 10 of the Fortune 500</a>. And what legal scholar <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/by/michelle-alexander">Michelle Alexander</a> calls “<a href="https://newjimcrow.com/">the New Jim Crow</a>” – the system of mass incarceration that disproportionately criminalizes people of color – is not confined to the South, but nationwide.</p>

<p>Old lines of difference between the South and the rest of the nation have faded. So have the once-common nicknames that described them – with the stubborn exception of “Bible Belt.” </p>

<p>A quick glance at the news shows its persistence, with headlines discussing “<a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/civicnation/2020/03/05/be-careful-little-ears-what-you-hear-reflecting-on-the-bible-belts-beliefs-about-women/">The Bible Belt’s Beliefs About Women</a>,” or describing one Arkansas town as “<a href="https://edition.cnn.com/2022/06/29/us/eureka-springs-lgbtq-arkansas-town-cec">the Bible Belt’s LGBTQ Oasis</a>.”
The cultural issues reported in stories like these are no doubt real, but framing them as expressions of an enduring Southern Bible Belt seems to imagine religion as unchanging, timeless.</p>

<p>In reality, both the region’s people and their religion are changing dramatically. More Black, Latino and biracial people live in the South than in any other part of the country. White people make up <a href="https://censusreporter.org/profiles/02000US3-south-region/">just 52.5% of the regional population</a>. The rapidly changing South is dynamic, second only to the West in demographic diversity.</p>

<p>This shapes religion, too. As the 2023-2024 <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/racial-and-ethnic-composition/hispanic/?_gl=1*6gpwyu*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..&amp;gclid=CjwKCAjw-rTUBhAiEiwADv8gBOSq2PH0AFbLjx60jl1nZp3NG_IXpZTMJ4vQQ60o-_EML1PsEa123RoCN8EQAvD_BwE&amp;gbraid=0AAAAA-ddO9EZ3uFThCgY51at2emqyCQSt">Pew Religious Landscape Study</a> showed, Black and Latino Americans are more likely than white Americans to identify as Christian. The faith of Black Southerners (predominantly Baptist) and Latino Southerners (predominantly Catholic) is a reminder that the South is not a religious monolith.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, white Baptists and Methodists are not the force they used to be. Their main institutions, the Southern Baptist Convention and the United Methodist Church, have been <a href="https://www.graphsaboutreligion.com/p/the-aftermath-of-the-schism-in-the">declining in membership for decades</a>. The same Pew study showed that a mere 12% of Southerners <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/region/south/?_gl=1*1woexxd*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..&amp;gclid=CjwKCAjw-rTUBhAiEiwADv8gBOSq2PH0AFbLjx60jl1nZp3NG_IXpZTMJ4vQQ60o-_EML1PsEa123RoCN8EQAvD_BwE&amp;gbraid=0AAAAA-ddO9EZ3uFThCgY51at2emqyCQSt">identify with either denomination</a>.</p>

<h2>From ‘Bible Belt’ to ‘culture wars’</h2>

<p>Internally, both denominations have had major splits on <a href="https://theconversation.com/southern-baptists-may-have-rejected-a-constitutional-amendment-opposing-female-pastors-but-that-does-not-mean-they-are-changing-their-views-on-womens-leadership-in-church-232541">whether women can be leaders</a> and whether to <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-68939591">recognize LGBTQ identities</a>. Such splits reflect divides that <a href="https://sociology.as.virginia.edu/people/james-hunter">sociologist James Davison Hunter</a> diagnosed in 1991 as “<a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/27357156">Culture Wars</a>.” </p>

<p>Consider his book’s subtitle, though: “The Struggle to Define America.” In these culture wars, the battlefield is the nation. The fighters are not regions, but political factions. What they’re fighting over is the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/24/opinion/sunday/chicago-protests-1968-culture-war.html">legacy of the social movements of the 1960s</a>: civil rights, women’s rights, gay rights, the environment.</p>

<p>The fact that the culture wars for America can be found in the contemporary South is a testament to just how much the once-distinct region participates in the dynamics of national life. Those wars may sound louder in the South than elsewhere, but that’s not the expression of a changeless Bible Belt; rather, it is the historical pattern that reactions are often strongest where change is most pronounced.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/285325/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pennsylvania is suing TikTok over ‘addictive’ features – but that’s messier than it sounds</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757320/original/file-20260901-50-o003rq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday is accusing TikTok of deceptive age ratings and addictive design features that harm children.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/teenager-holds-a-phone-whose-screen-displays-the-tiktok-news-photo/2201533029?adppopup=true">VINCENT FEURAY/AFP Collection via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced <a href="https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/taking-action/attorney-general-sunday-announces-lawsuit-against-tiktok-for-misrepresentations-that-permit-age-13-rating-in-app-stores/">a civil lawsuit against TikTok</a> on Aug. 11, 2026, filed in Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas and accusing the social media platform of violating state consumer protection laws in ways that harm youth.  </p>

<p>There are <a href="https://cdn.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026-08-10-Pennsylvania-TikTok-Complaint.pdf">two central charges</a>. </p>

<p>One is deceit: for example, making false statements about how much of TikTok’s content contains mature themes, and about the ability of its guardrails to protect youth from that content. </p>

<p>The second alleges that “TikTok knowingly created platform features intended to cause excessive, compulsive, and addictive use, despite knowing that young people are more susceptible to – and acutely harmed by – those features.” Those features include infinite scrolling, autoplay and push notifications <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/17579139251331914">designed to trigger</a> the release of dopamine, the neurotransmitter that drives the brain’s reward system.</p>

<p>The company rejects the charges. In <a href="https://penncapital-star.com/children-families/ag-dave-sunday-sues-tiktok-for-misrepresenting-suitability-for-pennsylvania-teenagers/">a statement to the Pennsylvania Capital-Star</a>, a spokesperson for TikTok said, “This lawsuit relies on misleading and inaccurate claims and deliberately ignores the concrete safety measures TikTok has voluntarily implemented to support the well-being of our community.”</p>

<p>I’m a public policy professor, not a lawyer, so I won’t predict who’ll win in court. But after nearly 40 years <a href="https://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty-research/profiles/caulkins-jonathanp">studying how addictive products are marketed</a>, I agree that goods and services that lead to compulsive behaviors – whether scrolling or smoking – deserve special scrutiny.  However, they do not fall neatly into binaries such as being addictive or not, or dangerous for youth but safe for adults. Lawsuits that find defendants liable or not liable risk imposing black-and-white distinctions on trade-offs that require nuanced thinking. </p>

<h2>Binary thinking doesn’t work</h2>

<p>There is a long history of binary thinking about addictive goods.  </p>

<p><a href="https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/bulletin/bulletin_1953-01-01_2_page004.html">Drugs such as heroin</a> were seen as dangerous and bad, so they were banned. </p>

<p>Most everything else was good, or at least neutral. The government might tax and regulate, but traditionally it does not focus on protecting consumers from the consequences of overindulgence. The health department may regulate what goes into a doughnut, but not how many doughnuts go into you.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large, ornate building sits at the end of a busy street." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757334/original/file-20260901-70-hbh14q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">State attorneys general, including Pennsylvania’s, are increasingly taking the lead on regulating companies accused of exploiting compulsive consumption.</span>
