<title>People with Tourette syndrome, like Billie Eilish, use everything in their power to suppress tics – this exhausting process is key to treatment</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755505/original/file-20260821-50-yf12qp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6566%2C4377&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many people with Tourette&#39;s suppress their tics until they can release them in a safe space.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/young-man-with-eyes-closed-making-face-royalty-free-image/2212002884?phrase=person%20blinking%20face&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Klaus Vedfelt/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Imagine trying not to blink, resisting the urge to sneeze or refusing to scratch an intense itch. For a short time, you can probably succeed, but the effort becomes increasingly untenable until the urge eventually wins. </p>

<p>People with Tourette syndrome describe tic suppression in a similar manner. Tourette syndrome causes tics, or <a href="https://theconversation.com/taboo-tics-like-shouting-curses-and-slurs-are-uncommon-in-tourette-syndrome-but-people-who-have-them-suffer-harsh-social-stigma-276721">repeated movements and sounds</a>, that a person cannot always control. These tics often come and go, change over time and may occur along with attention problems, anxiety or obsessive-compulsive behaviors.</p>

<p>Some people with Tourette’s can temporarily control tics, such as during a public interview, but that does not mean tics are voluntary. Nor does it mean the person is faking their diagnosis. Rather, suppression can be a hallmark of the disorder and, ironically, has become one of the foundations of modern treatment.</p>

<p>Yet suppression can come at a cost.</p>

<p>I have seen this firsthand <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YXrkisUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">as a neurologist</a> who has been treating people with Tourette syndrome for over 20 years. Many of my patients have told me that while they can temporarily hold back tics through intense concentration, they later need to release them. They say it’s an exhausting process.</p>

<p>Understanding the neuroscience behind tic suppression and people’s experiences with it can help those without the disorder better recognize – and have compassion for – the dynamic and sometimes demanding symptoms of Tourette syndrome.</p>

<h2>Misunderstanding Tourette’s</h2>

<p>When singer-songwriter <a href="https://theconversation.com/billie-eilish-and-tourettes-our-new-study-reveals-what-its-really-like-to-live-with-the-condition-119570">Billie Eilish publicly acknowledged</a> in 2019 that she lives with Tourette syndrome, internet commentators responded in two ways: Some <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/may/06/billie-eilish-suppress-tourette-syndrome-tics-amy-poehler">expressed support</a>, while others <a href="https://www.boredpanda.com/billie-eilish-accused-pretending-neurological-disorder-tics-during-interview/">questioned whether her tics were real</a>.</p>

<p>Skeptics pointed to interviews or performances where she appeared to have no visible tics. Many concluded that she must be exaggerating or even faking her condition. But in a May 2026 interview on “Good Hang With Amy Poehler,” Eilish shared how <a href="https://youtu.be/Ja3_9BQXFf4?t=4632">suppressing her tics</a> requires constantly using “everything in (her) power” to do so. </p>

<p>Many people with Tourette syndrome often deal with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s1474-4422(22)00303-9">anxiety</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-443-13554-5.00024-9">obsessive-compulsive symptoms</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-443-13554-5.00003-1">attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder</a>, among other challenges, that have a far greater impact on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-07009-y">quality of life</a> than the motor or vocal tics themselves.</p>

<p>These invisible symptoms <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s1474-4422(22)00303-9">frequently interfere</a> with friendships and school performance. A child may be teased because of involuntary blinking or shoulder movements, but what ultimately limits that child’s success may be untreated anxiety, overwhelming obsessive thoughts or difficulty sustaining attention in the classroom. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Billie Eilish stands on stage in front of a crowd and holds a microphone." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755302/original/file-20260820-50-xhrchn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Billie Eilish, who has been open about living with Tourette syndrome, performs in Stockholm, Sweden.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/stockholm-sweden-billie-eilish-performs-at-avicii-arena-on-news-photo/2211678835">Samir Hussein/WireImage via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What causes Tourette’s is still unknown, though researchers believe <a href="https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/tourette-syndrome">genetics and environment</a> may play a role in its development.</p>

<h2>Unpacking tics</h2>

<p>Tourette syndrome affects <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pediatrneurol.2022.08.010">less than 1% of children worldwide</a>, although estimates vary across studies and populations.</p>

<p>While the disorder occurs around the globe, no two people experience Tourette syndrome in the same way. Some people have simple motor tics, such as blinking, shoulder shrugging or facial movements. Others <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11910-016-0633-x">have complex movements</a> involving multiple muscle groups or elaborate sequences of actions. </p>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/taboo-tics-like-shouting-curses-and-slurs-are-uncommon-in-tourette-syndrome-but-people-who-have-them-suffer-harsh-social-stigma-276721">Vocal tics</a> may range from throat clearing and sniffing to repeating words or sounds. Some people develop rituals or repetitive behaviors that overlap with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-443-13554-5.00024-9">obsessive-compulsive symptoms</a>, making it difficult to distinguish where a tic ends and an obsessive-compulsive behavior begins. </p>

<p>The condition <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-443-13554-5.00011-0">exists on a spectrum</a>. Each person’s combination of symptoms is unique.</p>

<p>People’s tics are also dynamic. They wax and wane and are influenced by <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2016.10.003">stress, sleep deprivation and illness</a>. Many people experience fewer visible tics while they are intensely focused on an activity, such as performing music or playing sports. Others say they have a dramatic increase in tics after returning home from school or work, where they can finally <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.parkreldis.2017.08.004">stop suppressing them</a>.</p>

<p>This fluctuation is one of the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s1875-9572(10)60050-2">defining characteristics of Tourette syndrome</a> and can lead outside observers to wonder whether a person’s diagnosis is real.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/759535923" width="500" height="281" frameborder="0" webkitallowfullscreen="" mozallowfullscreen="" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Some people with Tourette’s have learned to suppress their tics to the point of invisibility.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Many tics <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2016.01.008">are suppressible</a>. People can suppress their tics for hours in situations where they fear embarrassment or judgment. Teachers or employers may conclude that the student or employee is fine. But once home, the person releases a storm of tics.</p>

<h2>Suppressing tics as treatment</h2>

<p>Suppressing tics can be distracting and exhausting, yet decades of research has shown that tic suppression <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.607">can be strengthened and used therapeutically</a>. </p>

<p>In 2019, the American Academy of Neurology recommended behavioral intervention as an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000007466">evidence-based treatment for Tourette syndrome</a>. Among these is a method called <a href="https://practicalneurology.com/diseases-diagnoses/movement-disorders/comprehensive-behavioral-intervention-for-tics/31642/">comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics</a>, which teaches people to recognize the earliest warning sensations that precede a tic, understand the situations in which tics occur, and develop competing responses that reduce tic frequency and severity.</p>

<p>For example, someone may feel a building sensation in the throat just before a throat-clearing tic. Using behavior intervention, they can learn to respond by slowly breathing through the nose while keeping the mouth closed, making it harder to perform the tic until the urge passes.</p>

<p>They aren’t simply holding in their tics. This therapy helps people harness the brain’s natural capacity for self-regulation in a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14737175.2019.1643236">healthier and more sustainable way</a>. Large clinical trials have shown that this treatment <a href="https://practicalneurology.com/diseases-diagnoses/movement-disorders/comprehensive-behavioral-intervention-for-tics/31642/">significantly reduces tic severity</a> for many children and adults. </p>

<p><a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/5554-tourette-syndrome">Other treatments</a> include medication, behavioral therapy and for a small number of cases a surgical therapy called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaneurol.2017.4317">deep brain stimulation</a>. </p>

<h2>Building awareness and compassion</h2>

<p>By allowing the public to see both her extraordinary talent and her neurological condition, Billie Eilish not only revealed a diagnosis but also contributed to a global conversation about what tics are and why they are so often misunderstood. </p>

<p>I believe public visibility reduces stigma, encourages families to seek evaluation earlier and <a href="https://www.huffpost.com/entry/billie-eilish-tourette-syndrome-interview_n_69fb65bce4b065a1677a5d4d">inspires young people living with Tourette’s</a>. It also motivates researchers like me to develop better treatments.</p>

<p>Awareness also includes understanding tic suppression. The ability to suppress tics does not make them voluntary or the Tourette syndrome less real. In fact, understanding the warning sensations and the ability to modify a person’s response to tics has helped inform treatment. </p>

<p>Understanding what people see, and, importantly, what people may not see, can be one of the most powerful ways to support those living with Tourette syndrome today and into the future.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287277/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Fox Foundation, the Parkinson Alliance, the Smallwood Foundation, the Tourette Association of America, and the UF Foundation.</span></em></p></content>

excerpt: Many people with Tourette's suppress their tics until they can release them in a safe space
body: Many people with Tourette's suppress their tics until they can release them in a safe space
Klaus Vedfelt/DigitalVision via Getty Images Imagine trying not to blink, resisting the urge to sneeze or refusing to scratch an intense itch
For a short time, you can probably succeed, but the effort becomes increasingly untenable until the urge eventually wins
People with Tourette syndrome describe tic suppression in a similar manner
Tourette syndrome causes tics, or repeated movements and sounds , that a person cannot always control
These tics often come and go, change over time and may occur along with attention problems, anxiety or obsessive-compulsive behaviors
Some people with Tourette’s can temporarily control tics, such as during a public interview, but that does not mean tics are voluntary
Nor does it mean the person is faking their diagnosis
Rather, suppression can be a hallmark of the disorder and, ironically, has become one of the foundations of modern treatment
I have seen this firsthand as a neurologist who has been treating people with Tourette syndrome for over 20 years
Many of my patients have told me that while they can temporarily hold back tics through intense concentration, they later need to release them

Understanding the neuroscience behind tic suppression and people’s experiences with it can help those without the disorder better recognize – and have compassion for – the dynamic and sometimes demanding symptoms of Tourette syndrome

Misunderstanding Tourette’s When singer-songwriter Billie Eilish publicly acknowledged in 2019 that she lives with Tourette syndrome, internet commentators responded in two ways: Some expressed support , while others questioned whether her tics were real
Skeptics pointed to interviews or performances where she appeared to have no visible tics
Many concluded that she must be exaggerating or even faking her condition
But in a May 2026 interview on “Good Hang With Amy Poehler,” Eilish shared how suppressing her tics requires constantly using “everything in (her) power” to do so

Many people with Tourette syndrome often deal with anxiety , obsessive-compulsive symptoms and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder , among other challenges, that have a far greater impact on quality of life than the motor or vocal tics themselves
These invisible symptoms frequently interfere with friendships and school performance

A child may be teased because of involuntary blinking or shoulder movements, but what ultimately limits that child’s success may be untreated anxiety, overwhelming obsessive thoughts or difficulty sustaining attention in the classroom
Billie Eilish, who has been open about living with Tourette syndrome, performs in Stockholm, Sweden
Samir Hussein/WireImage via Getty Images What causes Tourette’s is still unknown, though researchers believe genetics and environment may play a role in its development
Unpacking tics Tourette syndrome affects less than 1% of children worldwide , although estimates vary across studies and populations
While the disorder occurs around the globe, no two people experience Tourette syndrome in the same way
Some people have simple motor tics, such as blinking, shoulder shrugging or facial movements
Others have complex movements involving multiple muscle groups or elaborate sequences of actions
Vocal tics may range from throat clearing and sniffing to repeating words or sounds
Some people develop rituals or repetitive behaviors that overlap with obsessive-compulsive symptoms , making it difficult to distinguish where a tic ends and an obsessive-compulsive behavior begins
Each person’s combination of symptoms is unique
They wax and wane and are influenced by stress, sleep deprivation and illness
Many people experience fewer visible tics while they are intensely focused on an activity, such as performing music or playing sports
Others say they have a dramatic increase in tics after returning home from school or work, where they can finally stop suppressing them
This fluctuation is one of the defining characteristics of Tourette syndrome and can lead outside observers to wonder whether a person’s diagnosis is real
Some people with Tourette’s have learned to suppress their tics to the point of invisibility
People can suppress their tics for hours in situations where they fear embarrassment or judgment
Teachers or employers may conclude that the student or employee is fine
But once home, the person releases a storm of tics
Suppressing tics as treatment Suppressing tics can be distracting and exhausting, yet decades of research has shown that tic suppression can be strengthened and used therapeutically
In 2019, the American Academy of Neurology recommended behavioral intervention as an evidence-based treatment for Tourette syndrome

Among these is a method called comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics , which teaches people to recognize the earliest warning sensations that precede a tic, understand the situations in which tics occur, and develop competing responses that reduce tic frequency and severity

title: A grim report card for the world’s schools
excerpt: A student takes the French general baccalaureate exam on June 15, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained,&nbs
body: A student takes the French general baccalaureate exam on June 15, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
A growing chorus of teachers, parents, and education experts is worried that American students can’t read

But, hear me out, silver lining here: At least the students are in good company . (Okay, maybe that’s not exactly a silver lining.) A new report from the Programme for International Student Assessment, or PISA — a standardized global test of 15-year-olds’ math, reading, and science skills, administered by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — finds that scores in all three subjects have dipped to their lowest levels in OECD countries since testing began in the early 2000s
Reading scores fell especially sharply, by the equivalent of more than a year of education, between 2015 and 2025

In the US, reading scores fell by roughly 14 percentage points between 2022 and 2025.  These results, based on a sample of more than 760,000 students from 91 countries, are among the most-watched educational metrics in the world

And the million-dollar question — as always — is why those metrics continue to fall.  The report gestures at the usual suspects: the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic; an attentional crisis that makes it difficult for kids ( and adults! ) to stick with long texts.  PISA also surveyed students about their use of generative AI, the first time it’s done so since the technology became widely available
But as I’ll explain more below, anyone looking for clear takeaways on classroom AI and its effect on learning will probably be disappointed
Go a little deeper View Link If you know a high school student, chances are they use AI for school
In the PISA report, 86 percent said they use it at least occasionally, and roughly one in 10 use it every day
But whether that helps or hurts learning seems to depend on how students use it
In this report, the small minority of students who never use AI generally outperformed those who do
But weekly users who used AI to “help them learn,” as opposed to using it to complete specific tasks, performed about as well as nonusers
And frequent AI users who were also taught AI literacy skills scored slightly higher

In other words, the unsatisfying answer to the question “Is AI good or bad for learning?” is probably…“it depends.” My colleague Adam Clark Estes took on this question last year, and found several promising applications of the technology in education: tools that free teachers from grunt work, for instance, and educational chatbots designed to provide personalized tutoring.  In upstate New York, where I’m based, a federally funded research center is developing AI tools for children with learning and language disorders
One mother told me she credited an AI reading app with dramatically improving her autistic son’s communication.  That nuance complicates the policy discussion around AI and education

Some of these applications would likely be disallowed under New York City’s new, one-year AI moratorium , for instance, which bans student-facing generative AI tools in public elementary and middle schools in the country’s largest district
In announcing the ban, schools chancellor Kamar Samuels argued a pause would allow the district to evaluate which tools, and which use cases, truly help students learn

That’s the assignment now facing educators and policymakers the world over — presumably, they won’t ask ChatGPT to do it for them.  One link for later ➨ Fight for your right to leave your phone at home
An ever-larger range of everyday tasks now requires a smartphone : reading a menu, parking a car, taking public transit, etc
But while the QR-codification of daily life can sometimes be convenient, it also locks many elderly and low-income people out of services and locks the rest of us into a cycle of digital dependence

Or consumer resistance.  Before you go… Did you know… that almost all of America’s walkable urban neighborhoods date back to before World War II ? In other words, you can live in a new house or apartment, or you can live in a walkable place

But most people won’t have the option to do both until the US builds denser urban housing.  Today’s trivia: In Greek and Roman mythology, who was the legendary founder and first queen of Carthage? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the archipelago that includes the Isle of Skye

That would be the Inner Hebrides, off the coast of Scotland, whose landscapes have inspired a wide range of cultural works: among them, the Enya song “ Ebudæ ,” the original screenplay for Peter Pan , and George Orwell’s 1984 .

title: Trump’s midterm strategy: More Trump
excerpt: The interior of the American Airlines Center is seen on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, on September 9, 2026. | Brand
body: The interior of the American Airlines Center is seen on the first day of the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas, on September 9, 2026. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is bound for Dallas to kick off Republicans’ midterm convention — which is likely to be all about him.  What’s going on? If you haven’t heard of a midterm convention before, you’re not alone

They’re not common: The last one was in 1982 and, as the New York Times notes , it “went so poorly” that a subsequent Democratic Party chair described them as “places for mischief” and canceled the next one
Nonetheless, Trump has decided to hold one this year to tout his and his party’s (but mostly his) record leading into the 2026 midterms
The event will span two days — today and Thursday — in Dallas, Texas, and Trump is set to get the prime speaking slot on both nights

The event won’t have any of the features that make a traditional presidential-year convention, such as formally selecting a candidate or setting a party platform; instead, it will look more like a multi-day GOP infomercial.  Is this a good strategy? If you’re a Republican politician, probably not

The Republican National Committee chair is explicitly billing the event as a “ Trumpapalooza ,” and with Trump in attendance, that’s what they’re sure to get.  The only problem is that polling suggests Trump is radioactively unpopular right now, with his overall approval hovering near record lows and dragging down Republican candidates across the board

Some Republican candidates are staying away from the convention entirely , while those who are attending may not see much benefit.  (Democrats, unsurprisingly, are thrilled by the Trump-centric convention, as the Washington Post reported on Wednesday.) How else is Trump getting involved in the midterms? He’s spending heavily, or at least starting to: His MAGA Inc. super PAC has about $400 million on hand and (indirectly) made $49 million in ad buys earlier this week in key states, plus another $10 million in Texas
He’s also asked voters to “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.” It remains to be seen whether that will yield the result he’s hoping for

And with that, it’s time to log off… We’re a few days past Labor Day, but here’s a fun Wall Street Journal story about the power of organized labor: How college football kickers, long an afterthought, “self-created their own market” to get paid in the NIL era
You can read it with a gift link here .  Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Republicans suffered a stunning Supreme Court loss. It lasted minutes.
excerpt: For once, Justice Brett Kavanaugh did the right thing
body: For once, Justice Brett Kavanaugh did the right thing

It may not matter. | Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images For several minutes on Tuesday evening, Democrats thought they’d actually scored an important legal victory — and in an election case to boot! But then a single Trump-appointed judge cast a cloud of doubt over that victory , and potentially threw Missouri’s upcoming congressional elections into chaos
Last Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court effectively halted a 2025 state law that would have redrawn the state’s congressional maps to give Republicans an extra seat in the US House

Republicans, along with Missouri’s Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, immediately ran to the US Supreme Court , hoping that the Court’s 6-3 Republican majority would order the state to use the new, more GOP friendly maps
But the Court didn’t just reject the GOP’s request, it did so in the most dismissive way possible
The Court’s order was exactly six words long — “ Application (26A304) denied by Justice Kavanaugh ” — and it notably was only attributed to one justice, Brett Kavanaugh

The Court’s procedures sometimes allow a single justice to dispose of a case, but the justices rarely invoke this process unless they view the matter as so one-sided that there’s no need to formally involve their colleagues
This case is known as Hoskins v. von Glahn
But then, just minutes after the ruling, Judge Stephen Clark, a federal district judge in Missouri, ordered the state to use the GOP-friendly maps after all
Though Clark’s case involves different parties — the lead plaintiff in Clark’s case is a Republican member of Congress, not Hoskins — the legal issues in both cases are virtually identical
And Clark’s opinion even acknowledges that, shortly before he ruled, Kavanaugh denied Republicans the very same victory that Clark wants to give them
Clark’s case, which is currently on appeal to the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, is known as Onder v
It’s the latest round of chaos to emerge from what is likely to be an unusually chaotic round of preelection litigation
Both Missouri cases arise out of the Republican Party’s decision to launch a gerrymandering war in advance of those midterms, a war that Democrats have fought back against with limited success

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump and his administration have also implemented several new policies that appear designed to skew the election toward the GOP, including Trump’s attempt to sabotage voting by mail , which is currently pending before the Supreme Court
It’s a terrible time, in other words, to be an election official
State election administrators should expect to spend the next two months buffeted by competing court orders, uncertain rules, and new policies that cannot possibly be legal

They should expect both Trump administration officials and state and federal judges to bombard them with commands that a ballot must be altered, or voters must be denied their right to vote — only to have those commands contradicted by new court orders that may themselves be tossed out on appeal
For now, for example, it’s unclear which maps Missouri is supposed to use in the upcoming midterms
And the final result in this case will likely turn on why Kavanaugh issued such a dismissive order in the Hoskins case

Kavanaugh may have ruled against Hoskins because Hoskins created the problem he wants the Court to solve In both Hoskins and Onder , Republicans raise three separate constitutional arguments that, they claim, require Missouri to use the new maps in this year’s midterms

The Hoskins case, however, is unique in that Denny Hoskins, the Republican elected official who formally sought the Supreme Court’s review in that case, may be the worst possible person to make such a request

Hoskins opens his brief to the Supreme Court with an alarming statement: “ A federal-election-administration disaster is unfolding in Missouri .” But as the state supreme court determined , this problem is entirely Hoskins’s fault
The man literally asked the US Supreme Court to save Missouri from a “disaster” that he created
Missouri’s Republican legislature enacted the new maps on September 12, 2025

However, under the state constitution, Missouri voters could trigger a ballot referendum on these new maps, provided that they submit “petitions signed by five percent of the legal voters in each of two-thirds of the congressional districts in the state” by a certain deadline

Opponents of the new maps met this deadline, submitting their petitions on December 9, 2025.  Significantly, the Missouri Constitution also provides that once a referendum is triggered, the law that is subject to the referendum does not take effect , and will not take effect unless it is approved by a majority of the state’s voters
So, under the state constitution, the new maps are not law, and they will not become law unless voters approve them in the upcoming general election

Thus, as the state supreme court noted in its unanimous opinion in Hoskins , “ this case involves a straightforward question of law .” The state constitution prevents laws subject to referendums from taking effect (with limited exceptions that don’t apply here), the state law creating the new maps are subject to a referendum, therefore that law is not in effect

But why did it take so long for the state supreme court to reach this straightforward result? The short answer is that opponents of the new maps asked the state court to rule sooner, but in a May 12, 2026 opinion, the Missouri Supreme Court determined that it could not rule on whether the new maps are in effect until after Hoskins issued his own ruling on whether a referendum was properly triggered — pointing to a state law that permits lawsuits to be filed in the 10 days after the secretary of state rules on the referendum

That May decision, however, also warned Hoskins that if the “petition filing is ultimately determined to be sufficient,” then that would mean that the new maps cannot be used in the 2026 election because the law authorizing those maps is not in effect

Nevertheless, Hoskins waited until August 4, the last possible date that he could rule on the petitions seeking a referendum — and also the date of the state’s primary election — to issue a ruling against the referendum
The state supreme court’s opinion from last Thursday holds that Hoskins was wrong to reject the petitions, and thus the new maps never took effect
We are now just two months from the November election, yet the state supreme court abruptly required Missouri to use different maps than the ones it used during the recent primary election

This situation is genuinely very bad, because it will be difficult for the state’s election officials to reshuffle voters into their correct congressional districts before the election takes place.  It also means that, assuming that the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision stands, some voters will vote in a different district than the one they voted in in the recent 2026 primary election
Incredibly, Hoskins actually argued in the state supreme court that it could not suspend the new maps so late in the game

As Judge Ginger Gooch wrote in response, this argument is “particularly misplaced given the secretary’s delay created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains .” So one possible explanation for Kavanaugh’s unexplained order ruling against Hoskins is that Kavanaugh did not believe that Hoskins had any business asking the Court to fix a problem that he created
Courts often rule against litigants who have “ unclean hands ,” meaning that they contributed to the problem they want the court to fix
But, if that’s the case, then it’s still possible that Republicans could prevail in Onder , because the plaintiffs in that case did not personally create the problems that the GOP now complains about

Alternatively, Kavanaugh may have ruled against the GOP because he thought their legal arguments are garbage The other possible explanation for Kavanaugh’s decision in Hoskins is that the justice believed that the GOP’s legal arguments were weak

title: America is built for driving. There’s hidden demand for something better.
excerpt: Maybe you’ve heard this unkind old joke about American culture: We will pay a small fortune to amble through the cobblestone streets of Rome and Paris, or even
body: Maybe you’ve heard this unkind old joke about American culture: We will pay a small fortune to amble through the cobblestone streets of Rome and Paris, or even the ersatz Main Street in Disneyland
Then we’ll return to our suburban homes and two-car garages, and swear that a place like that could never work here.  There’s a sad truth to this
In cities and suburbs across the country, a vocal contingent of Americans devote themselves to resisting change that could bring denser, more pedestrian-oriented development to their backyards

Many people I talk to about my work on American cities share the sense that streets built around walking might be a charming holdover for societies enlightened enough to preserve them, but sprawl-loving Americans simply don’t want to live that way

Earlier this year, Pew published a survey that seemed to confirm this: “Majority of Americans prefer spread-out communities with big houses.”  But that framing was unfortunate, because it emphasizes precisely the wrong takeaway about Americans’ preferences for how they want to live.  Pew’s own data, along with other evidence on the question, suggests there’s substantial pent-up appetite for a walking-friendly way of life in the US — and not nearly enough supply of places that can satiate it.  There are many reasons it’s hard for us to build that way in the 21st century, but a simple lack of demand isn’t one of them

Our shortage of places designed for walking reflects one of the most tangible but rarely voiced domains in which Americans lack freedom and choice.  In the land of the free, it should not be so hard to walk to buy a little treat! And building more places where the pleasures and necessities of daily life are close at hand does not mean eliminating the lower-density, driving-oriented communities that many other Americans prefer

Walking has a surprisingly large constituency The top-line claim from Pew’s nationally representative survey is correct: 55 percent of the 8,512 respondents said they prefer to live in a place where “houses are larger and farther apart, but schools, stores and restaurants are several miles away.”  But the more interesting and telling finding is how many said the opposite: 44 percent of Americans  — approaching half the country! — would rather live where homes are “smaller and closer to each other, but schools, stores and restaurants are within walking distance.” That number is much higher than the share of Americans who can actually meet their daily needs on foot — and a country split 55–44 on how it wants to live shouldn’t be built overwhelmingly for the 55 percent

An analysis from Smart Growth America, a nonprofit that advocates for compact, mixed-use development, finds that 6.8 percent of Americans live in walkable communities in the country’s 35 biggest metro areas

A separate 2025 study , meanwhile, estimated that only 10.8 percent live in places designated “most walkable” by the EPA.  View Link Other surveys have found an even larger constituency for neighborhoods where daily errands don’t require a car

In a recent survey by the National Association of Realtors (NAR), using a sample of 2,000 adults in the 50 largest US metro areas, 59 percent said they prefer “houses with small yards, and it is easy to walk to the places you need to go.” The remaining 41 percent would choose “houses with large yards, and you have to drive to the places where you need to go.”  One result that particularly surprised me from NAR’s poll, given America’s strong cultural affinity for single-family homes, was that respondents were evenly split between these two options:  “Own or rent an apartment or townhouse and you have an easy walk to shops and restaurants and have a shorter commute to work,” chosen by 52 percent of poll takers.  “Own or rent a detached, single-family house and you have to drive to shops and restaurants and have a longer commute to work,” chosen by 48 percent.  An earlier survey, analyzed by researchers at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, similarly found that 55.7 percent of adults “reported favoring (36.3%) or strongly favoring (19.4%) community design with stores and other destinations within walking distance even if homes are closer together.” Public opinion polling can be an imperfect indicator of what people actually want — an issue I’ll return to

A 2024 survey from the National Association of Home Builders points to some of those complications: Two-thirds of participants said they consider a walkable community “desirable” or “essential.” But two-thirds also said they prefer a detached single-family house, and most indicated they prefer to live in suburbs, both of which can be somewhat in tension with walkability
This survey didn’t ask respondents what they’d trade off (like home size) to live within walking distance of everyday destinations, so it offers fairly weak evidence for how highly they prioritize it

But I could find no major national survey in which walkability was a fringe taste; even when asked to trade it against bigger homes, bigger yards, or detached housing, the walkable option consistently attracts a large percentage — and often a majority — of Americans

These findings tap into a sense that the way we build our surroundings in the US has gotten badly out of whack. “It’s antisocial,” one American tourist said in a video that went viral this summer, as he walked through Munich in wonder at the vibrant public realm around him
Walking is not an anachronistic transportation technology, but rather the native scale of human life
It is “the intentional act closest to the unwilled rhythms of the body, to breathing and the beating of the heart,” author Rebecca Solnit wrote in her book Wanderlust

A built environment conducive to walking, unsurprisingly, causes people to walk more, and traveling on foot can turn a nightmare commute into a more pleasant and salutary experience, among myriad other benefits.  But housing in such places is in desperately short supply because much of (probably almost all) of America’s walking-oriented urban fabric dates to before World War II, and we’re doing little to expand it.  Walkability is popular
The trade-offs needed to achieve it are not
As with opinion polling on lots of other issues, there are limits to how literally we can take these surveys
They involve weighing hypothetical scenarios that most people aren’t accustomed to thinking about

Many respondents may have never given much thought to walkability before, and so might be coming up with an answer on the spot rather than retrieving a stable internal preference.  And the surveys also don’t ask about perhaps the most significant trade-off required by walkable communities
Compact development built around walking is geometrically incompatible with designing everything around the automobile
So making walking easier also requires making driving and parking less cheap and convenient

Opinion polling suggests Americans don’t feel favorably about congestion pricing , and many people (even in the most walking-friendly cities in the US) freak out when unlimited free parking is threatened, as journalist Henry Grabar documented in his book Paved Paradise

So the mere fact that people say they want walkability does not mean it would be easy to create in places built around driving — we can’t have both. (This is analogous to other politically difficult ideas, like the debate over single-payer healthcare — the proposal polls well , and it’s indeed a good idea! But it’s  much   harder  to get voters to accept the big tax hike that it calls for, even if it means they’d no longer need to pay private insurance premiums.)    Nevertheless, one need only look at the stratospheric real estate prices in America’s relatively few walkable areas to see that demand to live there is extremely high
With rare exceptions, we don’t build new neighborhoods like this anymore, and haven’t in decades

Although the US is often singled out as uniquely bad at prioritizing humane and liveable built environments, car-dependent development has become the norm for new communities built across much of the world since the mid-20th century, including in European suburbs
We might one day recover the lost art of building human-scale places
Until then, the simplest way to meet millions of Americans’ desire for that way of life is for existing walkable cities and suburbs to permit more housing

If high-demand places like New York City, Boston, San Francisco, Seattle, and their inner-ring suburbs added more density, it is certain that more people would move there (and this need not happen only through high-rises, which are disliked by many Americans)

Doing so would also help alleviate our housing affordability crisis, while ensuring that these desirable places are replenished with new homes compatible with modern life, rather than just decrepit Victorians and walk-up apartments.  Imagine if the roughly half of us who say we want to be able to walk to meet our daily needs could live somewhere that made it possible — it would mean a dramatic transformation in the texture of American life

But that change need not come at the expense of people who prefer something else — the point is to create more choices, not fewer, and Americans who want more space, privacy, and to drive for most trips would remain perfectly free to choose that way of life.  So if Greenwich Village is not your idea of heaven on Earth, no one will force you to live there.

title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia

body: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August : one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey

title: This founder is teaching chips how to recycle (their energy)
excerpt: Throughout the history of the computer chip, engineers have treated waste heat as an inevitable cost of a calculation
body: Throughout the history of the computer chip, engineers have treated waste heat as an inevitable cost of a calculation
Hannah Earley, however, thinks it’s a design choice
Earley, 31, is cofounder and chief technology officer of Vaire Computing, a startup building chips that recycle energy usually thrown away as heat—a strategy known as reversible computing
Ultimately, she thinks, this approach could help make data centers (and our laptops and phones) much more energy efficient
When conventional computer chips perform calculations, they erase the information they no longer need along the way, dissipating energy as heat in the process
Earley compares the approach to racing through a city only to pump the brakes at every intersection: The car loses momentum and must burn more fuel to accelerate again

Reversible computing aims to keep the momentum going—instead of erasing information from the intermediate steps in a calculation, the circuit retains it, making it possible to run the computation backward and recover some of the energy
While the idea was first proposed more than 50 years ago, it proved impractical to implement with existing transistors and circuits
Earley, though, has completely rethought the hardware needed to make energy recovery work
She designed a patent-pending type of resonator—a microscopic chip component that stores recovered energy for later reuse. “It’s really a glorified pendulum,” she says
Last year, Vaire announced a key breakthrough: a chip with a resonator that recovered more energy than it lost, even after the energy needed to power the component was taken into account

For a subfield that has existed mostly in theory, the result was proof of life. “It’s clear they have something interesting,” says Igor Markov, a researcher in electronic design automation and a former professor at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

Still, he says, the technology is quite early stage; the company will need “a series of increasingly realistic and convincing demonstrations to attract the industry support needed for commercialization.”  She gradually became convinced that the connection between information, energy, and heat could change computers forever
Earley’s journey into chip design started sooner than most
She began programming around the age of nine, starting with high-level coding for the web before digging into other programming languages like Perl and Java
She continued progressing to more and more abstract layers of computing, until she got all the way down to transistors
She eventually enrolled in a PhD program at the University of Cambridge under the computational biologist Gos Micklem
She started out studying how materials such as DNA could be used to perform calculations, but a few months in, Micklem sent her the 1999 PhD thesis of Michael Frank, a pioneer in reversible computing
Earley read it once, felt skeptical, read it again, and sat with it for a few weeks
She gradually became convinced that the connection between information, energy, and heat could change computers forever
The fascination completely redirected her PhD work

Earley studied the physical limits of computation and built software that could turn ordinary programs into reversible ones. “Eventually I wouldn’t let her put my name on any of her papers, because I felt that I couldn’t really stand up and give a proper talk about them,” Micklem recalls. “It was her stuff.” After completing her degree in 2021, Earley met Rodolfo Rosini, a technology entrepreneur and investor

The pair cofounded Vaire that same year, and the company has since raised more than $12 million, hired Frank as a senior scientist, and begun turning the vision of reversible computing into real hardware
Innovation, however, doesn’t happen overnight

During the winter of 2022 in Grinnell, Iowa, Earley spent weeks in her now-wife’s basement apartment as the wind chill outside reached roughly −40 °F, covering a whiteboard over and over again with schematics for the core piece of circuitry needed to make reversible logic work

By the time the design finally came together, after the couple had escaped the cold for Las Vegas, it felt less like an aha moment and more like a gradual wave of relief. “I’m not completely out of my depth,” she remembers feeling.  Earley and her colleagues’ next challenge is making their drastically different chip fit into familiar devices and manufacturing systems

She believes that’s where the future lies—not in further refining existing chips but in rebuilding them from the ground up with an eye toward reversibility. “I want to tackle every part of how computers are built,” Earley says, “and rethink it in these terms.”

title: Trump’s Smithsonian vendetta, briefly explained
excerpt: Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution Lonnie Bunch speaks during an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on February 20, 2026, in Was
body: Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution Lonnie Bunch speaks during an event at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on February 20, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: The head of the Smithsonian Institution will resign after weathering nearly two years of attacks by President Donald Trump.  What’s happening? Lonnie G

Bunch III, the secretary of the Smithsonian, announced on Tuesday that he will step down at the end of 2026 after more than seven years in the role.  Bunch’s retirement isn’t entirely about Trump; he’s 73 and has already served longer as secretary than his two most recent predecessors

But the president, who has waged a relentless campaign against what the White House has described as “improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology” at the Smithsonian, is indisputably part of the story

As Bunch put it to the New York Times on Tuesday, “at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.” What has Trump done to the Smithsonian? Since last spring , Trump has gone after the Smithsonian system for promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive.” He has threatened its funding, forced out the director of the National Portrait Gallery, and attempted to meddle with its exhibits
His ability to successfully make changes has been limited by the Smithsonian’s structure — but a new secretary could give Trump far more control

The president also, unsurprisingly, wants more Trump: administration officials have reportedly pressed for a new Portrait Gallery exhibit focusing on the president .  What’s next? Trump doesn’t officially have a role in selecting Bunch’s successor, who will be chosen by the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents — but that board does include Vice President JD Vance and multiple Republican members of Congress, so he might as well

Trump will surely want to install a loyalist, which means — as the Washington Post’s art and architecture critic Philip Kennicott explained on Tuesday — that the Smithsonian’s fate could depend on the ability of the rest of the board, and especially its chancellor, Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, to resist

And with that, it’s time to log off… Don’t miss my colleague Rachel Cohen Booth’s new piece on the “smartphone trap” : the way in which phones have become not just ubiquitous, but required for many parts of daily life (reading a menu, parking a car, signing into an account — the list goes on).  As Rachel argues, it’s not too late to preserve, or claw back, the option of going through life phone-free. “Pushing for a non-smartphone option is about accessibility, affordability, and agency
It’s about demanding the kind of freedom in a society we deserve to have,” she writes.  You can read her full story here with a gift link — enjoy, and we’ll see you right back here tomorrow!

title: Why Iowa is a state to watch in the midterms
excerpt: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand greets members of the audience during a campaign visit to the Cass County Community Center in Cass, Iowa, on August
body: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand greets members of the audience during a campaign visit to the Cass County Community Center in Cass, Iowa, on August 20, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images Can a love-thy-neighbor, stop-the-division campaign win over masses of rural voters? Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor in Iowa, has his hopes pinned on it.  Key to Sand’s campaign is a promise to end the red-blue warfare in politics

He’s made embracing independents and disgruntled Republicans a core part of his campaign, in addition to ending government corruption, holding big agriculture and big chemical companies responsible for the state’s high cancer rates, and addressing cost-of-living concerns
And his pragmatic approach seems to be working
Polls have reliably shown Sand, who currently serves as Iowa state auditor, ahead of his Republican opponent, Zach Lahn — despite the GOP’s significant voter registration advantage
Democrats haven’t won the governor’s mansion in Iowa since 2006
On top of the gubernatorial race, Iowa also has competitive Senate and House races , which could be key to Democrats’ hopes of gaining control of Congress during this November’s midterm election

To break down what’s happening in Iowa, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Laura Belin, publisher and reporter for the Iowa political website Bleeding Heartland .  Noel and Belin discussed Sand’s unique candidacy, whether it could have lessons for other Democrats looking to succeed in Midwestern states that have grown redder, and how President Donald Trump’s policies could be laying the groundwork for a rural backlash in this year’s midterm elections
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
This midterm season, all eyes seem to be on Iowa
Why is Iowa so crucial? What has happened in Iowa, where we used to be a swing state and we’ve moved into the red column, is not unique to Iowa
Every part of the country that looks like Iowa has seen the same trend of voters moving away from Democrats

It’s happened especially in these working-class communities where the electorate is predominantly white people without a college degree.  Iowa as a whole voted for Barack Obama twice and then voted for Donald Trump three times

So if Democrats can figure out how to start winning again, or at least losing by less, in that kind of area, it could have implications not only for the future of Iowa, but for other states like Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania
What are the main issues that people there are voting on and campaigns are campaigning on? The high cost of everything is definitely the top issue

Democrats have really been hammering on the tariffs and the war in Iran, driving up the cost of everything.  Also, healthcare costs have skyrocketed.  We’ve seen healthcare access be an issue, because we’ve already seen some clinics close, and the companies that control those hospitals or clinics have talked about how it’s partly a reaction to the big Medicaid cuts that were passed in the [GOP’s 2025] budget reconciliation bill
According to many polls that I’ve seen, Trump is underwater in Iowa
His policies are not popular; the tariffs are not popular in Iowa
They’re widely understood to be hurting the Iowa economy
Anyone can see that the cost of everything has gone up
What are the Democrats doing to campaign on that? Are they running on Trump? Most of the Democrats are not running directly against Trump
Rob Sand, the candidate for governor, hardly talks about Donald Trump at all
He really focuses on statewide issues.  Josh Turek, the candidate for Senate, is running [on] the idea that [Republican Senate nominee] Rep
Ashley Hinson has just been a rubber stamp for policies that have hurt Iowa, whether that be the war in Iran [or] tariffs
It’s more running against the Republicans who have been a puppet [for Trump] rather than running against Donald Trump himself
Let’s talk about that governor’s race and Rob Sand
This guy has gotten a fair bit of national interest
What do you know about him? I’ve followed his career for a long time, since he was running for state auditor the first time in 2018
He’s gone out every year, done a hundred town halls a year, done them in every county.  He is reaching out to independents because Iowa Republicans have a pretty large voter registration advantage
So he’s talked a lot about trying to empower independents more in our political spaces
He’s talked about getting Iowa back to divided government
He’s talked about how, with the large Republican majorities we have in the legislature, he would be a check on what they’ve done with 10 years of one-party rule
He used to be a model.  A long time ago, when he was in college
It’s funny, Republicans post these old modeling photos of Rob Sand from the ’90s and even [Sen.] Chuck Grassley’s campaign account posted some of those over the weekend
And I always wonder — I mean, Republicans seem to think that they’re going to get traction out of that, but I don’t really see that as something that Iowans care about at all
I think a more common criticism that I hear is that Rob Sand has a very strong social media presence and has for years

In addition to making videos talking about political issues and what needs to be done in state government, he does a lot of things like reviewing pizza and donuts.  They try to portray him as someone who’s not serious about his job
But I think that that’s just more [that] he has this goofy online persona
And I don’t really think it’s a detriment to his campaign
We’ve seen a certain type of Democrat emerge in the last few years and become very visible this campaign cycle: angry at the Democratic Party, angry at the direction of the country

title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
excerpt: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brough
body: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week
The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period
In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas
A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region
More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas
At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes
On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing
